lessons.title: Motor Mounting Bracket Installation
lessons.body:
The motor mounting bracket is the backbone of your EV motorbike's drivetrain. It must hold the motor firmly, align with the rear wheel sprocket, and withstand constant vibration on rough African roads. Start by identifying the correct bracket for your motor typeâmost hub motors need a swingarm bracket, while mid-drive motors require a custom frame plate. Use 4mm to 6mm thick steel; aluminium bends too easily under load. If you don't have a pre-made bracket, cut one from a steel plate using an angle grinder. Measure the motor's bolt hole spacing (commonly 100mm or 120mm) and drill matching holes with a drill press or hand drill. Deburr all holes with a file.

Before welding or bolting the bracket to the frame, mock-fit the motor. The motor shaft must be parallel to the rear axle, and the sprockets must line up within 1mm. Use a straight edge or string line to check alignment. If the bracket is welded, tack-weld first, check alignment again, then complete the weld. For bolted brackets, use M10 or M12 grade 8.8 bolts with nyloc nuts and washers. Tighten to 40-50 Nm for M10 and 70-80 Nm for M12. Add a second bracket or gusset if the motor weighs more than 10kg to prevent flex.

In Africa, dust and water are constant enemies. After installing the bracket, paint it with anti-rust primer and a top coat. Check that the bracket does not interfere with the chain or belt. Spin the motor by handâit should turn freely without rubbing. If you hear scraping, adjust the bracket. Finally, ride the bike slowly for 100 metres and re-check all bolts. Vibration will settle the bracket, so re-torque after the first ride. A well-installed bracket lasts for years; a poor one cracks and destroys your motor.

lessons.title: Aligning and Torquing Motor Bolts
lessons.body:
Motor bolts are the only thing keeping your motor from spinning off the bracket. Loose bolts cause vibration, stripped threads, and eventually a broken motor casing. You need a torque wrenchâborrow one if you don't own it. For M8 bolts, use 20-25 Nm; for M10, 40-50 Nm; for M12, 70-80 Nm. Always use new nyloc nuts or thread-locking compound like Loctite 243. Never reuse old nuts that have lost their nylon insert.

Alignment starts before you tighten anything. Insert all bolts finger-tight. Check that the motor shaft is perpendicular to the bracket face. Use a square or a machined block to verify. If the motor tilts, shim it with stainless steel washersânever use soft metal or rubber. For hub motors, the axle flats must sit fully in the dropout slots. If the axle is too short, do not force it; get the correct axle length. For mid-drive motors, ensure the motor sprocket and rear sprocket are in line. A misalignment of more than 1mm will wear out the chain in a few hundred kilometres.

Tighten bolts in a star pattern, like you would a cylinder head. First pass: 50% of final torque. Second pass: 100%. This prevents warping the bracket. After torquing, mark each bolt and nut with a paint pen so you can see if they move. Ride the bike for 10km, then re-check torque. Most bolts will need a small extra turn. Check again after 100km and then every 500km. In dusty conditions, bolts can loosen faster. Carry a spare set of bolts and a small torque wrench on long trips. If a bolt strips, drill it out and use a helicoil insertâdo not just use a bigger bolt.

lessons.title: Controller Placement and Heat Sink Setup
lessons.body:
The controller is the brain of your EV motorbike. It must be mounted where it gets airflow but is protected from water, mud, and direct sun. The best place is under the seat or on the frame downtube, facing forward so air hits the heat sink fins. Never mount it upside downâwater will pool inside. Use rubber grommets or silicone pads between the controller and frame to reduce vibration. Vibration kills controllers faster than heat.

Most controllers have an aluminium heat sink. If yours is small, add a larger heat sink using thermal paste and M4 screws. Clean both surfaces with alcohol first. Apply a thin, even layer of thermal pasteâtoo much is as bad as too little. For African heat, consider adding a 12V computer fan blowing across the fins. Wire the fan to the controller's 12V output or a separate switch. Keep the fan intake clean; dust clogs it quickly. If you ride in mud, mount the controller higher, above the rear wheel splash zone.

Cable entry points must face down or sideways, never up. Use dielectric grease on all connectors to keep water out. After mounting, check that the controller does not touch any moving parts. Leave at least 20mm clearance from the tyre and chain. Test the temperature after a 15-minute ride: if the controller is too hot to touch (above 60Â°C), improve airflow or reduce current. A cool controller lasts longer and delivers more power. In the rainy season, cover the controller with a breathable coverânot plastic, which traps moisture. Check mounting bolts every month; a loose controller can crack its circuit board.

lessons.title: Wiring Motor Phase Cables
lessons.body:
Motor phase cables carry heavy current between the controller and motor. They are usually three thick wiresâyellow, green, and blueâbut colour codes vary. What matters is that each controller phase matches the correct motor phase. If you mix them up, the motor will run rough, overheat, or not turn at all. Start by identifying the motor's phase wires. Use a multimeter on continuity: touch two motor phase wires together and spin the wheelâit should feel stiff. That confirms they are paired. Label them A, B, C with tape.

Strip 10mm of insulation from each cable. Use a proper crimping toolânot pliersâto attach ring terminals or bullet connectors. Solder the crimp for extra strength if you have a soldering iron. Cover the joint with heat shrink tubing, then wrap with self-amalgamating tape for waterproofing. Route the cables away from sharp edges and hot parts. Use cable ties every 150mm. Do not run phase cables alongside the throttle or hall sensor wiresâthey cause interference. If you must cross, cross at 90 degrees.

Connect the phase cables to the controller. The order matters: if the motor runs backwards, swap any two phase cables (e.g., yellow and green). If it stutters, you have a wrong combinationâtry different pairings until it runs smooth. Never disconnect phase cables while the controller is powered; it can blow the MOSFETs. After wiring, check resistance between each phase and the motor casingâit should be infinite. Any reading means a short. Test the bike on a stand first. If the motor gets hot quickly, recheck phase order. Use 10 AWG or 8 AWG silicone wire for motors above 1000W. In Africa, buy extra cableâcheap wire overheats and melts.

lessons.title: Connecting Controller to Battery and Motor
lessons.body:
This is the high-voltage step. Before you connect anything, turn off the battery and remove the fuse. Use a multimeter to confirm zero volts at the battery terminals. Connect the main battery positive (red) to the controller's B+ terminal, and negative (black) to B-. Use ring terminals crimped and soldered. Tighten with a spannerâdo not overtighten, or you will crack the controller's plastic housing. For 48V systems, use 10 AWG wire; for 72V, use 8 AWG. Add an inline fuse (40A for 1000W, 60A for 2000W) on the positive cable within 200mm of the battery.

Next, connect the motor phase cables as described in the previous lesson. Then connect the hall sensor plug (usually a 5-pin connector). If your motor has no hall sensors, ignore this. Connect the throttle: three wiresâred (5V), black (ground), and green or white (signal). Never connect the throttle to battery voltage; it will burn out. Connect the brake cut-off switch if your controller supports it. This cuts power when you brake, saving energy and improving safety.

Before powering up, double-check every connection. Look for stray wire strands touching other terminals. Turn on the battery. The controller may beep or show an LED. If nothing happens, check the fuse and the ignition wire (often a thin red wire that needs to be connected to battery positive). If the motor spins when you push the throttle, you are good. If it spins immediately without throttle, your throttle is wired wrong or the controller is faulty. Test all lights and the brake cut-off. After a 5-minute test ride, check all connections for heat. Warm connectors mean loose or undersized wiring. Re-torque battery terminals after the first ride.

lessons.title: Initial Controller Parameter Setup
lessons.body:
Your controller comes with factory settings that may not match your motor, battery, or riding conditions. You need a programming cable or a Bluetooth module and a smartphone app (like Kelly or Sabvoton). If you don't have one, borrow from a local EV shop. First, set the battery voltage. For a 48V lithium battery, set low-voltage cut-off at 42V and high-voltage cut-off at 58V. For lead-acid, set low cut-off at 44V. Never set low cut-off below 40V for 48V systems, or you will damage the battery.

Next, set the rated motor current. This is the continuous current the controller can send. For a 1000W motor at 48V, that's about 20A. Set the peak current to 1.5 times rated (30A) for 10 seconds. Too high and you overheat the motor; too low and you lose power. Set the phase current to 2.5 times rated (50A). If your controller has a

as appropriate. For hub motors, set the pole pairs (usually 23 or 46). Count the magnets in your motor and divide by 2.

Set the throttle response to

for beginners. Set the max speed to match your gearingâstart at 40km/h and increase gradually. Enable regenerative braking if your controller supports it, but set it to low (10-20%) first. Test the bike on a stand. Check that the motor does not stutter at low speed. If it does, adjust the hall sensor angle or reduce phase current. Save the settings to the controller. After a 10km ride, check motor and controller temperatures. If either is too hot, reduce current by 10%. Write down your final settings and keep them for future reference. In Africa, dusty conditions mean you should set a lower current to extend motor life.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended thickness for a steel motor mounting bracket?
quiz.explanation: 4mm to 6mm steel is recommended to withstand vibration and load without bending.

quiz.q: When aligning the motor sprocket with the rear sprocket, what is the maximum allowable misalignment?
quiz.explanation: Misalignment over 1mm will cause rapid chain wear.

quiz.q: What type of nut should be used on motor mounting bolts?
quiz.explanation: Nyloc nuts have a nylon insert that resists loosening from vibration.

quiz.q: What torque should be applied to M10 grade 8.8 motor bolts?
quiz.explanation: M10 bolts typically require 40-50 Nm for proper clamping force.

quiz.q: Why should you tighten motor bolts in a star pattern?
options: B) To prevent warping the bracket
quiz.explanation: A star pattern distributes pressure evenly and prevents bracket distortion.

quiz.q: What should you do if a motor bolt strips its threads?
options: B) Weld the bolt in place
C) Drill and install a helicoil
D) Leave it and add glue
quiz.explanation: A helicoil insert restores the thread to the original size and strength.

quiz.q: Where is the best place to mount the controller on an EV motorbike?
options: A) Under the seat facing forward
quiz.explanation: Under the seat facing forward gets airflow and protection from water and mud.

quiz.q: What should be applied between the controller and an additional heat sink?
quiz.explanation: Thermal paste improves heat transfer between surfaces.

quiz.q: Why should cable entry points on the controller face down or sideways?
quiz.explanation: Facing down or sideways stops water from entering the controller.

quiz.q: What is a sign that the controller is overheating?
options: A) It is too hot to touch (above 60Â°C)
B) It makes a clicking sound
quiz.explanation: Controllers should run cooler than 60Â°C; higher temperatures indicate poor airflow or excessive current.

quiz.q: How can you identify paired motor phase wires using a multimeter?
options: B) Check continuity while spinning the wheel
quiz.explanation: When two phase wires are connected, spinning the wheel feels stiff due to shorting.

quiz.q: What is the correct tool for attaching ring terminals to phase cables?
quiz.explanation: A crimping tool makes a proper mechanical connection; pliers can damage the terminal.

quiz.q: If the motor runs backwards after connecting phase cables, what should you do?
options: A) Swap any two phase cables
B) Swap all three phase cables
quiz.explanation: Swapping any two phase cables reverses the direction of a three-phase motor.

quiz.q: What wire gauge is recommended for phase cables on motors above 1000W?
quiz.explanation: 10 AWG or 8 AWG silicone wire handles the high current without overheating.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid running phase cables alongside throttle wires?
quiz.explanation: High-current phase cables can induce noise in sensitive signal wires.

quiz.q: What should you do before connecting the controller to the battery?
options: B) Remove the fuse and confirm zero volts
quiz.explanation: Safety first: ensure no voltage is present before making connections.

quiz.q: What size inline fuse is recommended for a 1000W, 48V system?
quiz.explanation: A 40A fuse protects the controller and wiring from overcurrent.

quiz.q: Which wire on the throttle is usually the signal wire?
quiz.explanation: Red is 5V, black is ground, and green or white carries the signal.

quiz.q: What does the brake cut-off switch do?
options: B) Cuts power to the motor when braking
quiz.explanation: It disables the motor during braking for safety and energy saving.

quiz.q: If the motor spins immediately when the battery is connected without touching the throttle, what is likely wrong?
options: A) The battery is too low
B) The throttle is wired wrong or faulty
C) The motor is too small
quiz.explanation: A shorted or miswired throttle can send a constant signal.

quiz.q: What is the low-voltage cut-off for a 48V lithium battery?
quiz.explanation: 42V prevents over-discharge and damage to the lithium cells.

quiz.q: For a 1000W motor at 48V, what is the rated continuous current?
quiz.explanation: Power divided by voltage gives current: 1000W / 48V â 20.8A, so about 20A.

quiz.q: What should the peak current be set to relative to rated current?
quiz.explanation: 1.5 times rated current for short bursts provides acceleration without overheating.

quiz.q: How do you determine the number of pole pairs for a hub motor?
options: B) Count the magnets and divide by 2
quiz.explanation: Pole pairs equal half the number of magnets in the motor.

quiz.q: What throttle response setting is recommended for beginners?
quiz.explanation: Smooth response gives predictable control and is safer for new riders.

quiz.q: What should you do after a 10km test ride regarding controller settings?
options: B) Check temperatures and reduce current if too hot
quiz.explanation: Monitoring temperature ensures the controller and motor are not overloaded.

quiz.q: Why is it important to write down your final controller settings?
options: B) For future reference and troubleshooting
quiz.explanation: Recorded settings help you restore or adjust the controller later.

quiz.q: In dusty African conditions, what adjustment helps extend motor life?
quiz.explanation: Lower current reduces heat and wear in harsh environments.

quiz.q: What should you use to waterproof electrical connections?
quiz.explanation: Self-amalgamating tape creates a watertight seal when stretched and wrapped.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a gusset on a motor mounting bracket?
options: C) To prevent flex and cracking
quiz.explanation: A gusset adds rigidity and strength to the bracket.
